newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel CPI fears push linked bond yields down.
newsitem.headline: Israel CPI fears push linked bond yields down.

text.p: Yields on Israeli CPI-linked bonds fell below four percent on Sunday as traders braced for Tuesday's release of the June consumer price index (CPI) and a period of higher inflation, traders said.
Indices:
* Government bonds general: +0.2 pct to 109.53
* CPI-linked government bonds: +0.27 pct to 109.26
* Unlinked government bonds: +0.08 pct to 109.72
* Dollar-linked government bonds: -0.03 pct to 111.4
* Bank of Israel short-term Makam bills: +0.09 pct to 107.77
Volume including Makams was a low 120 million shekels.

"The market is waiting for the June CPI," said Gidi Halpern of Meitav Investments and Securities. "The index is very unpredictable because no one is sure what effect the depreciation of the shekel has had on inflation."
"Forecasts are that the CPI will be between 0.2 to 0.9 percent. Before the rise of the dollar forecasts were that it would be around 0.3 percent," he said.

After the government instituted changes in the exchange rate mechanism and the Bank of Israel slashed interest rates on June 18, the shekel fell sharply against the dollar. The shekel has since been trading nervously.
Halpern said traders bought CPI-linked bonds out of fear that the higher dollar would fuel inflation in the coming two months.
"Yields on CPI-linked long bonds are at a two-year low today, around 3.95 percent," Halpern said. "All things being equal, we expect yields to fall to 3.6 percent in the coming months."

He said CPI-linked bonds also rose because of the improved situation in the capital market and because liquid provident funds had to buy them. Halpern added that the market was also influenced by a slowdown in new Treasury issues.
On Thursday, the Bank of Israel said it would not issue any CPI-linked bonds this week but only unlinked bonds for a total of 150 million shekels, noted Gila Shkury of Israel Discount Bank.

Halpern said it is widely believed that the budget deficit would rise after the summer, which would force the government to step up borrowing. Nevertheless, he said, the market was still behaving as if supply would be tight.
Demand for unlinked bonds was higher as well from traders who thought the inflationary impact of the exchange rate would be slight.
"Despite the rise of the dollar, its impact on inflation will be minor because the economy is in a slowdown," Shkury explained.
Trading in dollar-linked bonds was stable with a lower trend, she said.
Note: Makams are zero-coupon unlinked certificates with durations of three months to one year. The Bank of Israel issues Makams to absorb liquidity.
($1 = 3.55 shekels)
